summary:
NISAR TerraScout is an independent Earth observation project combining satellite data, earthquake reports and geospatial analysis. Its interactive world map brings together recent USGS earthquake reports, NISAR acquisition footprints from NASA’s Alaska Satellite Facility DAAC, and candidate surface-change regions from the project’s processing pipeline.

The earthquake recorder displays recent USGS ComCat events as clickable map markers. Each marker can show the reported magnitude, location, depth, coordinates, update time and a link to the USGS record. The feed refreshes periodically, providing an updated view of reported seismic activity. Earthquake details come from USGS; NISAR observations are a separate data source and are not live earthquake measurements or alerts.

The Python pipeline processes local NISAR HDF5 datasets, identifies candidate changes and exports results for the map. Users can search the ASF archive by country, date range and product level, or explore worldwide coverage.

In a future phase, a rover could investigate selected locations at ground level. An accelerometer, soil-moisture sensor and camera could record local shaking, soil conditions and images, adding field observations to the satellite-scale view. This would extend TerraScout from mapping potential areas of interest to collecting complementary measurements on site.
details:
NISAR TerraScout — Team Zyravix

NISAR TerraScout is a geospatial project for exploring changes in Earth’s surface. It processes local NISAR HDF5 observations through a Python pipeline that applies data-quality filters, converts radar measurements to decibels, compares observations over time, and groups unusual pixels into candidate regions. These results can be viewed on an interactive map alongside NISAR archive footprints. The project also displays recent earthquake reports from the USGS ComCat feed, with details such as location, magnitude, depth and report time. Earthquake reports and NISAR observations are separate sources: NISAR is not a live earthquake detector or alert system.

The project aims to make complex satellite data easier to explore and help users identify places that may merit further investigation. It uses publicly available NASA–ISRO NISAR data archived through NASA’s Alaska Satellite Facility DAAC, along with official USGS earthquake reports. NASA NISAR · USGS GeoJSON feeds

The current prototype uses Python, NumPy, pandas, SciPy and rasterio for processing and geospatial outputs; Tkinter/CustomTkinter for the desktop interface; and HTML, CSS and JavaScript for interactive map features. It also uses tools such as Folium and MapLibre for mapping.

Its creative direction is to connect a broad satellite view with place-specific event information—and eventually ground observations. A future Raspberry Pi rover could carry an accelerometer, soil-moisture sensor, camera and GPS to collect timestamped, geotagged measurements near selected sites. This rover is a planned concept, not a built or tested system.

The team considered data quality, spatial and temporal alignment, uncertainty and false positives, coverage limits, and the need to distinguish candidate changes from confirmed events.
